title: Efficacy of downhill running training for improving muscular and aerobic performances
authors: Toyomura J, Mori H, Tayashiki K, Yamamoto M, Kanehisa H, Maeo S
population: 18 healthy young males; -10% downhill (n=10) vs level (n=8) running, 20 min x 3 sessions per week for 5 weeks at the heart rate associated with lactate threshold
findings: At similar heart rate (77.7% vs 76.4% HRmax) the downhill group ran faster (14.5 vs 12.0 km/h).
Downhill training raised knee extension torque by 9-24% at all angular velocities and improved change-of-direction time by 2-3%, with no change in other parameters.
Level training raised VO2max by 5%, improved energy cost at lactate threshold by 3% and raised velocity at VO2max by 7%, with no change in other parameters.
The authors conclude that downhill training has little effect on aerobic capacity compared with heart-rate-matched level training.
limitations: 18 young males, 5 weeks, unequal group sizes. The abstract does not say participants were randomised, so the design is treated as a small controlled trial. Aerobic tests were on level ground; no trail-race outcome.
implications: Use downhill running (about -10%) as a strength-specific stimulus for knee extensors, not a substitute for aerobic work; keep level or uphill running for aerobic development.

The studied dose was 20 min x 3 per week for 5 weeks at lactate-threshold heart rate in young men. Treat it as a research dose, not a prescription for unaccustomed runners; introduce it gradually (see the repeated bout effect papers).

verification.notes: Crossref: Appl Physiol Nutr Metab 43(4):403-410, 2018, six authors match. PubMed PMID 29182895 abstract supports all numbers. Downgraded B to C and design to controlled-trial: abstract does not mention randomisation and n=18. Removed unsupported 'rest day' advice.
